title: Sustainable solar greenhouse drying of tomatoes: Kinetic modeling and environmental burden reduction
content:
Abstract

The novelty of this study is the application of a dynamic dual-mode aeration system (DDMA) within greenhouse solar dryers for tomato drying. The system was evaluated using two greenhouse solar dryer (GHSD) configurations, namely a flat-roof GHSD and a gable-roof GHSD, with tomato samples prepared as 6 mm slices, quarters, and halves under salted and unsalted conditions. The dryers were compared with open sun drying (OSD) under Aswan, Egypt climatic conditions, where solar radiation ranged from 108 to 880 W/m2, ambient temperature from 24 to 42.3°C, and wind speed from 0 to 0.2 m/s. Drying behavior was strongly affected by dryer configuration, sample geometry, and salt pretreatment. The gable-roof GHSD provided the fastest moisture removal, particularly for salted slices, which reached approximately 8.06% w.b. within 10 h, corresponding to a 44.4% reduction in drying time compared with OSD. The peak drying rate reached approximately 4.5 g water/g dry matter·h for salted slices in the gable-roof GHSD. Effective moisture diffusivity ranged from 0.58 to 2.65 × 10−10 m2/s in the flat-roof GHSD and from 0.70 to 2.84 × 10−10 m2/s in the gable-roof GHSD. Water-removal productivity reached up to 0.140 kg water/h, while normalized carbon-emission mitigation reached 1.608 kg CO2-eq/batch per 1 kWh kg−1 water. Thin-layer modeling showed strong agreement between experimental and predicted moisture-ratio data. These findings indicate that DDMA-assisted GHSDs can provide a practical low-carbon route for tomato drying and offer a basis for future scale-up, quality optimization, and integration with renewable-energy-based postharvest processing systems.
